explanations.answer: Rebuke the people who brought them
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The disciples rebuked the ones carrying the little ones in. Moms and dads show up with kids hoping for a blessing, and they get a scolding instead. I think those folks were not expecting that at all.

explanations.answer: Line the children up for Him
explanations.explanation: I'd love to tell you the disciples set up a nice orderly line, but that's not what happened. The text says the disciples rebuked those who brought the children. So nobody got organized, they got scolded. I think the line would have been a much better plan.

explanations.answer: Carry the children to Jesus themselves
explanations.explanation: Nope, the disciples weren't doing any carrying. The people were the ones bringing the children, and the disciples rebuked them for it. Somebody wanted those little ones near Jesus, and it wasn't the disciples in that moment.

Right on the money, baker. Jesus says, “…For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” He points at the very children the disciples were shooing off. Jesus gives them the reason, and it's the kids themselves.

I can see why you'd think that, friend, because rule-keeping sounds impressive. But that's not what Jesus says here. He says the kingdom of God belongs to such as these, and He's pointing at little children. Nobody in that crowd was handing the kids a rulebook.

Teachers of the law don't come up in this scene, baker. Jesus is looking at the little children when He says, “…For the kingdom of God belongs to such as these.” The ones the disciples tried to turn away are the ones He names.

Close, but Jesus says the opposite. He says, “Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” Never, friend. So receiving it like a little child is not a side option.

Yes, this one is False. Jesus says, “Truly I tell you, anyone who does not receive the kingdom of God like a little child will never enter it.” A little child just receives, with open hands. That's the way Jesus says to come.

True, and what a scene. After all those words, Jesus took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them. The very thing the people came for, they got. I think those little ones went home carried by more than their parents.
This one is True, friend. The text says Jesus took the children in His arms, placed His hands on them, and blessed them. The people who brought them got exactly what they came for, and then some.

explanations.answer: What he must do to inherit eternal life
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The man runs up, kneels, and asks, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?” He's serious about it. People don't sprint and kneel over a small question.

explanations.answer: Which commandment is the most important
explanations.explanation: Good guess, but the man doesn't ask about the commandments. It's Jesus who brings them up after the man's question. The man asks what he must do to inherit eternal life, and that's the whole reason he came running.

explanations.answer: Where Jesus will be teaching next
explanations.explanation: No schedule questions here, friend. The man asks Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Now that's a question worth running for, and kneeling for.

explanations.answer: He has kept all of them since his youth
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. He says, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” That's quite a claim, and the text gives no hint that Jesus argues with him about it. Next comes Jesus looking at him with love.

explanations.answer: He has broken most of them over the years
explanations.explanation: Nope, this man is not confessing a pile of broken commandments. He says all of them he has kept from his youth. Honestly, I'd have mumbled and changed the subject.

explanations.answer: He has never been taught all of them
explanations.explanation: The man doesn't say he missed any lessons, friend. He says, “Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.” He knows the list and he says he's kept it.
That's right, friend. Jesus says to sell everything he owns and give to the poor. Then he'll have treasure in heaven. It's a big ask, and Jesus says it looking at him with love.
The temple isn't in this verse, baker. Jesus says to go, sell everything he owns, and give to the poor. Then comes the promise of treasure in heaven.
Priests don't get a mention here, friend. Jesus tells the man to sell everything he owns and give to the poor. The treasure He promises is in heaven.

Yes, and it's a heavy moment. The text says the man was saddened by these words and went away in sorrow. Jesus had just invited him to come follow Him, and he walked off the other way. I think this one hurts.

explanations.answer: Sells it all that same day
explanations.explanation: That's not how it goes, baker. The man was saddened and went away in sorrow. The text never says he sold anything. He left, and that's where his part of the story stops.

explanations.answer: Asks for more time to decide
explanations.explanation: The man doesn't ask for time, friend. The text says he was saddened by Jesus' words and went away in sorrow. No answer, no goodbye in the text, just a sad walk away.
That's the word, baker. The man went away in sorrow because he had great wealth. Jesus had just told him to sell everything he owned. That's a lot to hold in your hands and hear that.
Debts would be a whole different story, friend. The text says the man had great wealth. That's why he was saddened by what Jesus said about selling everything he owned.
The text doesn't mention doubts, baker. It says he went away in sorrow because he had great wealth. And Jesus had just told him to sell everything he owned.
True, friend. The text says the disciples were amazed at His words. Jesus had just said, “How hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God!” They hadn't seen that coming.
This one is True, baker. After Jesus said how hard it is for the rich to enter the kingdom of God, the disciples were amazed at His words. They did not just nod along.

explanations.answer: A camel passing through the eye of a needle
explanations.explanation: That's the picture, friend. Jesus says, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.” A camel is a big animal and a needle's eye is tiny. Jesus is making it clear this is hard.

explanations.answer: A boulder floating across the Jordan River
explanations.explanation: A floating boulder would be quite a sight, baker, but Jesus doesn't say that. He says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. A camel and a needle, that's the picture.

explanations.answer: A tower built all the way up to the sky
explanations.explanation: No towers in this passage, friend. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle. That's the picture He gives for how hard it is for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.
That's the one, baker. They said to one another, “Who then can be saved?” If a camel and a needle made them nervous, I get it. Jesus has an answer coming for them.

explanations.answer: Why did the rich man leave
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to wonder, but it's not what they ask. The disciples say to one another, “Who then can be saved?” Their question is bigger than one man leaving.
I can see why you'd think that, friend, since they had just heard about selling everything. But the text shows a different question. They say to one another, “Who then can be saved?”

Yes, baker. Jesus says, “With man this is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.” The disciples asked who can be saved, and Jesus points them to God. That's a good answer to hang onto.
Time doesn't do it, friend. Jesus says, “With man this is impossible, but not with God.” Waiting longer isn't the answer here. God is.
Angels don't come up in this answer, baker. Jesus says, “With man this is impossible, but not with God.” He looks right at the disciples and points to God.

explanations.answer: A hundredfold in houses and family and fields
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jesus says anyone who leaves home or family or fields for His sake and the gospel will receive a hundredfold in the present age. He lists houses, brothers and sisters, mothers, children and fields. And in the age to come, eternal life.

explanations.answer: A crown to wear on the last day
explanations.explanation: A crown is not in Jesus' answer, baker. He says a hundredfold in the present age, with houses and family and fields. And in the age to come, eternal life.

explanations.answer: Nothing at all until the age to come
explanations.explanation: Jesus says the opposite, friend. He promises a hundredfold in the present age, not just later. Then in the age to come, He adds eternal life.

Hold on, friend, Jesus doesn't leave that part out. He says a hundredfold in the present age, “…houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, along with persecutions…” So the persecutions come along with the blessings. Jesus doesn't hide that.

Yes, this is False, baker. Jesus says the hundredfold comes “…houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and fields, along with persecutions…” The promise is real, and so is the part about persecutions. Jesus tells them both.
Right, baker. Jesus says, “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.” Notice He says many, not all. That flips how people usually think about who's in front.
You'd think so, friend, since first sounds like the winner's spot. But Jesus says many who are first will be last. Then He turns it around: the last will be first.
Tests don't show up in this verse, baker. Jesus says, “But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.” First becomes last, and the last become first.
